_provenance: Peer-reviewed papers verified 2026-08-26 via the PubMed MCP tool (convert_article_ids + get_article_metadata) against real PMID/PMCID/DOI records - not accepted from any prompt-provided claim. Technical/regulatory/manufacturer documents reused from data/raw/trend_corpus.json, already individually fetched and archived in an earlier session (data/real_raw/trend_sources/). See research.md for the full query log.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Real-World Effectiveness of Portable Air Cleaners in Reducing Home Particulate Matter Concentrations
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Lu FT, Laumbach RJ, Legard A, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Does a portable air cleaner's benefit reach rooms beyond the one it sits in?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: PM2.5/PM10 fell 78.8%/63.9% in the primary room and 57.9%/60.4% in a secondary room during the filter condition vs. sham.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: A single PAC measurably reduces PM in the room it occupies and, to a lesser degree, an adjacent room, especially with a central air handler running.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That secondary-room reduction generalizes to homes without central air handling, or to non-COVID-positive households.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: Lab CADR ratings describe one sealed room; this trial shows real homes leak filtered benefit unevenly.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Room-sizing guidance should not assume the treated room is airtight from the rest of the home.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if a purifier were rated by whole-home effect, not single-room CADR?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: n=23-29 per measure; homes of COVID-positive adults only; secondary-room effect depended on HVAC use.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Reduction of personal PM2.5 exposure via indoor air filtration systems in Detroit: an intervention study
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Maestas MM, Brook RD, Ziemba RA, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.journal: Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Double-blinded randomized crossover intervention, 40 senior participants
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Do cheaper HEPA-type filters reduce personal PM2.5 exposure nearly as well as true-HEPA?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: True-HEPA cut personal PM2.5 exposure 53% and indoor concentration 60%; a cheaper HEPA-type filter still cut exposure 31% and concentration 52%.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Both high- and low-efficiency portable filtration measurably reduce personal PM2.5 exposure for older adults, not just indoor air readings.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That the gap between true-HEPA and HEPA-type performance is negligible for all pollutant sizes or health outcomes.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: A materially cheaper filter class still delivers most of the exposure reduction - performance may be commoditizing faster than price.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Filter-grade marketing claims should be checked against personal-exposure data, not indoor-concentration data alone.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if Versuni competed on verified personal-exposure reduction instead of filter-grade branding?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: n=40, Detroit seniors only; 3-day exposure windows per condition; no clinical outcome measured.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Effectiveness of portable HEPA air cleaners on reducing indoor PM2.5 and NH3 in an agricultural cohort of children with asthma: A randomized intervention trial
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Riederer AM, Krenz JE, Tchong-French MI, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Randomized intervention trial, 71 households (36 HEPA, 35 control)
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Do HEPA cleaners lower both PM2.5 and ammonia in farmworker children's homes with asthma?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: HEPA homes had 60% lower sleeping-area and 42% lower living-area PM2.5 at one year; ammonia reductions were not observed.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Sustained (one-year) PM2.5 reduction is achievable with two placed units in real agricultural-community homes.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That reduced PM2.5 translated into fewer asthma symptoms - no clinical/symptom endpoint was reported in this result.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: A pre-filter marketed to also cut ammonia measurably failed to do so, while PM2.5 reduction held - not every co-benefit claim survives a field trial.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Multi-pollutant marketing claims (e.g. 'also reduces odors/gases') need their own field evidence, not an inference from PM performance.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if a product only claimed the pollutant classes it has field evidence for, by room?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: No symptom/clinical outcome reported in this measure; single agricultural region; ammonia source strength not characterized.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: PM10, PM2.5, PM1, and PM0.1 resuspension due to human walking
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Full-scale laboratory chamber experiment, controlled carpet/dust loading
peer_reviewed_papers.question: How much does ordinary walking resuspend settled particles back into room air?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: 10 minutes of walking measurably raised PM10/PM2.5/PM1/PM0.1 concentrations, with estimated resuspension rates reported per size fraction.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Human movement over a loaded carpet is a real, measurable indoor particle source, not just deposition.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That a floor-level or mobile purifier would outperform a conventional room-level purifier - this study did not test any purifier placement.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: Standard room-level filtration treats air as the whole problem; this shows the floor is an active, re-triggered source, not a sink.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Spatial-source modeling for sizing/placement should not assume particles, once deposited, stay deposited.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if treatment intervened closer to floor-level resuspension events, not just ambient room air?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Single controlled chamber, one carpet type and dust load; not a real-home field study; no purifier tested.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Self-reported health impacts of do-it-yourself air cleaner use in a smoke-impacted community
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Turner MW, Prathibha P, Holder A, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Pilot phased-intervention study, tribal community, n=10 (wildfire) + n=17 (wood stove)
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Does using a low-cost DIY air cleaner during smoke events change self-reported symptoms?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: No association was found between DIY air-cleaner usage and self-reported symptoms; usage itself was low, and loud operating noise was cited as a barrier to use.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: In this small pilot, noise was a real, named reason people ran the device less than intended.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That air cleaners don't help symptoms in general - the sample was too small and usage too inconsistent to draw a causal conclusion either way.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: A device only helps if it is actually run - noise-driven under-use can erase a filtration benefit that lab tests would predict.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Adherence (will the device actually stay on) is a design variable, not a footnote to filtration performance.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if the product optimized for hours-actually-run under real noise tolerance, not peak CADR?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: n=10 and n=17, self-reported symptoms, low DIY-unit usage limited statistical power; not generalizable beyond this community.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Analysis of sources and sinks of indoor particulate matter reveals insights into the real-world efficacy of portable air cleaners in a randomized intervention trial
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Farhoodi S, Kang I, Jagota K, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Randomized parallel-group intervention trial, year-long, ~55 Chicago homes analyzed to date
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Do simple before/after PM averages correctly show whether a portable air cleaner is working?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: Raw averages misleadingly showed higher PM in the active-filtration group (higher source strength homes); background-period PM was ~36% lower with active filtration, and loss rates rose ~15-130% with fan speed.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Fan-speed-dependent loss rates, not raw before/after averages, are the credible way to show PAC efficacy in an unbalanced real-home sample.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That every home in the active group experienced the same benefit - source-strength imbalance between groups means simple averages cannot be trusted.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: Naive interpretation of real-world PM averages can make a working purifier look ineffective - the sizing/performance claim depends entirely on the analysis method.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Any real-world performance claim needs a source-adjusted or background-period analysis, not a raw before/after comparison.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if the product reported its own loss-rate estimate instead of a single CADR number?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Interim analysis (55 of a larger planned sample); one US metro area (Chicago); veteran-population-skewed cohort.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: The impact of portable air cleaners on indoor particulate matter concentrations and perceptions of indoor air quality: a randomized crossover trial in three multifamily buildings
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Mendell AY, Lee S, Siegel JA
peer_reviewed_papers.journal: Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Three-arm randomized crossover trial (placebo/constant/auto), 60 apartments, 3 Toronto buildings
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Does automatic (threshold-triggered) operation clean as well as running a purifier constantly?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: Constant operation cut weekly mean PM2.5 by 66% (95% CI 59-72%); auto operation cut it by 40% (95% CI 27-50%) but sharply reduced runtime.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Auto mode trades measurable filtration effectiveness for much less runtime; measured performance diverged from theoretical CADR-based sizing.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That one control strategy (always-constant or always-auto) is optimal for every home - the paper explicitly says a universal strategy may not fit.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: Constant operation filters more air but runs longer (noise, energy); auto runs less (quieter, cheaper) but filters measurably less.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Sizing guidance built on theoretical CADR should be corrected against this measured constant-vs-auto gap, not assumed equivalent.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if the 'right' operating mode were chosen per household noise tolerance rather than shipped as one factory default?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Multifamily buildings in one city (Toronto); one-week arms per condition; self-reported behaviour data alongside sensor data.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Indoor environmental health and asthma relief: findings from a longitudinal HEPA filter trial
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Li L, Lv X, Jia H, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.journal: Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part A
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Randomized controlled trial, 100 adults with moderate-to-severe asthma, 8-month follow-up
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Does 8 months of real HEPA H14 filtration measurably improve asthma control, not just air readings?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: The active group gained +2.2 Asthma Control Test points and +27.7% symptom-free days versus placebo, alongside a 29.6 microg/m3 PM2.5 drop (all p<=0.004).
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: In this one RCT, sustained HEPA H14 filtration is associated with a measurable clinical asthma-control benefit, not only an air-quality change.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That this specific effect size generalizes beyond this single trial - treat as a candidate finding requiring independent replication before treating as settled.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: This clinical result sits in tension with RP-03 and RP-05, where PM/exposure reduction did NOT translate into a measured symptom benefit - the literature is not unanimous on this link.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: A health-outcome marketing claim needs its own replicated clinical evidence; PM-reduction evidence alone is insufficient (see science-says/does-not-say framing).
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if Versuni ran or co-funded an independent replication before making any asthma-relief claim?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Single-center trial, self-reported symptom-free days as one endpoint, needs independent replication; journal is a niche toxicology/engineering title, not a primary respiratory-medicine venue.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Low-cost sensors for indoor air quality monitoring: A systematic review of accuracy, applications, and limitations
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Silva G, Duarte J, Baptista JS, Rufo JC
peer_reviewed_papers.journal: Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: PRISMA systematic review, 24 studies screened from 2,736 identified
peer_reviewed_papers.question: How accurate are the low-cost sensors that consumer air purifiers use to sense and react?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: Many low-cost sensors correlate well with reference instruments under controlled conditions, but performance varies significantly with humidity, temperature, and pollutant source; most devices don't yet meet formal regulatory validation standards.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Low-cost PM/CO2 sensing is workable for consumer devices but context-dependent, and current products largely lack standardized validation.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That any specific consumer purifier's onboard sensor is accurate enough to safely drive fully autonomous decisions in all conditions.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: More onboard sensing sounds like more intelligence, but this review's own finding is that sensor trust, not sensor presence, is the open problem.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: A 'smart'/reactive control claim should disclose the conditions under which its sensor reading is and isn't trustworthy.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if the most valuable smart feature is the product knowing when to distrust its own sensor?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Review of PM2.5/CO2 sensors specifically; heterogeneous underlying study methods; regional/device coverage bias noted by the authors themselves.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Validating the performance of low-cost IAQ sensors through co-location
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Zaky N, Li T, Stopps H
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Co-location validation against reference instruments, 2 consumer-grade sensors
peer_reviewed_papers.question: When two consumer-grade IAQ sensors are placed next to lab-grade references, how well do they agree?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: One consumer sensor tracked relative CO2/PM changes well (higher correlation) but showed higher bias/RMSE (lower absolute accuracy) than the reference; averaging over longer intervals improved but did not eliminate the gap.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: A consumer sensor can be precise (consistent, good for trends) while still being inaccurate (wrong absolute number) at the same time - these are different properties.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: That either tested sensor is reliable enough for uncalibrated absolute-concentration claims without in-situ calibration.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: A device can look 'smart' by tracking relative changes well while still reporting a materially wrong absolute air-quality number.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Any on-device number shown to a consumer should be understood (and ideally labelled) as relative-trend-grade or calibrated-absolute-grade, not treated as equivalent.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if the UI showed confidence/trend instead of a bare number the sensor cannot actually guarantee?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Two specific consumer sensor models only; one co-location site; short 5-30 minute averaging windows tested.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: Toward Better and Healthier Air Quality: Global PM2.5 and O3 Pollution Status and Risk Assessment Based on the New WHO Air Quality Guidelines for 2021
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Liu J, He C, Si Y, et al.
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Observational analysis of daily outdoor PM2.5/O3 monitoring data, 618 cities worldwide, 2019-2022, assessed against the WHO's 2021 Air Quality Guidelines
peer_reviewed_papers.question: Against the WHO's tightened 2021 PM2.5/O3 guideline, how much of the world's urban population still lives with unhealthy ambient air, and where?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: Across 618 cities (2019-2022), only ~10% of days globally met the new WHO PM2.5 guideline (<=15 ug/m3); over 35% of cities show compound PM2.5-O3 pollution; exposure-risk categories are markedly worse for cities in China/India than for economically developed cities.
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: Ambient/outdoor PM2.5 exposure against the tightened 2021 WHO guideline remains widespread globally - a demand-context fact (a large population is still exposed to guideline-exceeding outdoor air), not a claim about any indoor air cleaner's effectiveness.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: Anything about portable/indoor air cleaner performance, sales, or consumer behaviour - this is outdoor ambient monitoring-station data only, with no purifier or indoor-environment measurement.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: The scale of unmet WHO compliance globally could be used to over-claim indoor-purifier necessity, when this evidence only supports 'ambient air pollution is real and widespread', not 'a purifier fixes it'.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: Category-relevance / demand-context evidence (why air treatment matters at all) should stay visibly separate from device-efficacy evidence (whether a specific purifier works) - this paper is the former, not the latter.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if messaging clearly separated 'the outdoor air quality problem is real and global' from 'this specific product measurably fixes your indoor air' - conflating the two overclaims from evidence that only supports the first?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: Outdoor monitoring-station data only, 618 cities, 2019-2022 - no indoor measurements, no purifier-brand data, no causal claim about any intervention.

peer_reviewed_papers.title: A Burning Issue: Wildfire Smoke Exposure, Retail Sales, and Demand for Adaptation in Healthcare
peer_reviewed_papers.authors: Han J, Li S, Wang Z.
peer_reviewed_papers.study_design: Retail-scanner-data econometric study linking local wildfire smoke exposure to retail purchases (air purifiers, bottled water, cold/cough/nasal remedies) with lagged effects. Economics journal - outside PubMed's biomedical scope, verified by direct fetch/archive rather than the PubMed API (see data/real_raw/trend_sources/repec_han_wildfire_retail.html).
peer_reviewed_papers.question: When wildfire smoke hits an area, does that show up as a genuine, measurable bump in real retail demand for air purifiers - and how long does it last?
peer_reviewed_papers.found: Wildfire smoke exposure increases retail sales of air purifiers, bottled water, and cold/cough/nasal remedies, with a documented lagged effect (smoke from prior weeks still elevates current-week sales).
peer_reviewed_papers.establishes: A review-volume or sales burst coinciding with a wildfire event is a genuine, external-shock-driven demand signal, not a data anomaly to discount by default - directly relevant to how this project's own burst-detection judgment calls should treat wildfire-coincident spikes.
peer_reviewed_papers.does_not_establish: Anything about product performance, review sentiment, or which brand/features people bought - this is an aggregate sales-volume study, not a product-quality or preference study.
peer_reviewed_papers.tension: A demand spike caused by an external environmental shock (wildfire smoke) can look identical in the data to organic, sustained category growth, but the two have very different implications for forecasting.
peer_reviewed_papers.design_consequence: External-shock-correlated demand bursts (wildfire smoke, and by analogy other acute pollution events) should be flagged and reasoned about separately from steady-state category trend, not folded into the same growth-rate estimate.
peer_reviewed_papers.counterfactual: What if seasonal/event-driven demand forecasting explicitly modelled wildfire-smoke exposure as its own input, instead of treating all demand growth as one undifferentiated trend line?
peer_reviewed_papers.limitations: US retail-scanner data only; sales volume is a purchase-intent proxy, not a satisfaction or efficacy measure; the paywalled full study was archived but only its accessible listing/abstract-level detail is used here.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: Air Cleaners and Air Filters in the Home
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: EPA does not certify or recommend specific brands. Establishes that portable air cleaners reduce but do not eliminate indoor pollution, and that source control/ventilation are the primary levers - filtration is a supplement. Supports category-relevance claims, not efficacy claims for any specific product.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: Room Air Cleaners Key Product Criteria (ENERGY STAR)
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: Defines the CADR / Integrated Energy Factor / ozone-limit criteria a device must meet to be ENERGY STAR certified. Supports claims about how purifier performance and energy efficiency are formally measured; does not itself establish market size or growth.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: Find a Certified Room Air Cleaner (AHAM Verifide directory)
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: Industry-body-run, independent third-party CADR testing program. Supports the claim that CADR is the standard cross-brand performance metric; is an industry association, not a fully independent scientific body - its members are the manufacturers being certified.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: List of CARB-Certified Air Cleaning Devices
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: California-specific mandatory certification since 2010; ozone limit 50 ppb. Explicitly does NOT evaluate overall pollutant-removal effectiveness or declare devices 'safe' - supports a narrow safety claim only, not a general efficacy claim.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: WHO Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality: Selected Pollutants
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: Covers 9 indoor chemical pollutants (benzene, CO, formaldehyde, NO2, PAHs, radon, etc.) for regulators and building professionals. Supports the health-relevance framing of indoor air quality broadly; does not evaluate or endorse any purifier product or technology. Note: 2010 publication - the oldest source in this corpus; cited for enduring pollutant-exposure framework, not for current market conditions.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: Air Quality Sensor (Matter device type specification)
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: Standards-body specification: Matter's Air Quality Sensor device type (PM1/PM2.5/PM10/CO2/NO2/VOC/CO/Ozone/Radon/Formaldehyde clusters), added as part of Matter 1.2's nine new device types. Corrects an earlier draft of this corpus which mis-cited 'Matter 1.4' - the air-quality device type was actually introduced in Matter 1.2, verified directly against this page. Supports a connectivity-standardization claim, not an adoption-rate claim.

existing_technical_regulatory.title: Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation - 2025-2030 working plan
existing_technical_regulatory.scope_note: Verified directly: this specific EU working plan names priority product categories as steel/aluminium, textiles, furniture, tyres, mattresses and 'a number of energy-related products' - it does NOT name air treatment or household appliances as a distinct 2025-2030 priority. Cited for the broader Ecodesign/ESPR regulatory direction (repairability score, recyclability requirements) that could reach the category later, not as evidence air treatment is already a named priority - an honest scope correction versus an earlier draft's unverified 'Ecodesign review' claim.

existing_manufacturer_and_industry.title: Philips Domestic Appliances launches first all-in-one air purifier with AI technology
existing_manufacturer_and_industry.scope_note: MANUFACTURER'S OWN PRESS RELEASE about the Philips Air Performer 3-in-1 - describes AI-driven sensing, Wi-Fi/app control (Air+ app), NanoProtect HEPA. Treated as a primary product claim, not independent validation of performance or of category-wide AI adoption - the brief's own instruction to 'treat a vendor promoting its own product differently from an industry body' applies directly here.

existing_manufacturer_and_industry.title: Dyson launches air purifier with new sensing technology to destroy potentially dangerous indoor pollutants
existing_manufacturer_and_industry.scope_note: COMPETITOR'S OWN PRESS RELEASE: solid-state formaldehyde sensing, claimed as more durable than gel-based sensors. A primary vendor claim about a competing brand's technology, useful for competitive/technology landscape context, not independently verified sensor-accuracy evidence.

existing_manufacturer_and_industry.title: The State of Home Connectivity 2025
existing_manufacturer_and_industry.scope_note: Census-weighted nationwide US survey, n=3,780 (3,606 complete), +/-1.6% margin at 95% confidence, fielded August 2025. Reports 68% of households had a Wi-Fi problem in the past 12 months, 18% daily. This is a GENERAL home-connectivity survey, not purifier-specific - it can only support a claim that home Wi-Fi reliability is a widespread category-agnostic friction, not a claim specific to smart air purifiers.
